text.p: A U.S. military plane flew 30 Americans and 24 other people out of troubled Brazzaville in the Congo on Tuesday but no decision was immediately made to evacuate Americans remaining there, the Pentagon said.

The Americans and third country nationals were flown to Libreville in Gabon on a C-130 that carried a small U.S. military assessment team to Brazzaville from Germany earlier in the day to prepare for any requested evacuation.
Defence Department officials said an estimated 64 Americans remained in the city, some trapped in their homes by gunfire between warring factions in advance of elections.

Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon told reporters that the assessment team of about a dozen communications specialists, security troops and planners arrived in the Brazzaville from Germany on Tuesday afternoon.
He stressed, however, that no request had been made by the U.S. Embassy to evacuate Americans.
"The situation there is quite chaotic now," he said, but added that the gunfire did not appear to be targeting Americans or other foreigners.
The United States on Monday called for a ceasefire between rival factions battling in the Congo capital and said it believed presidential elections could still be held on schedule on July 27.
Bacon praised French troops in the city for helping provide security and evacuating some Americans earlier.

"We are relying now on the French for security in the area and also to help escort some of our people to the airport or out of the country," he said. "The French have been performing very well and have been extremely helpful."
Bacon said any evacuation would not be handled by the U.S. Navy helicopter ship Kearsarge, recently used to remove some 2,500 people -- including about 450 Americans -- from Freetown in Sierra Leone.

The Kearsarge is now in the Canary Islands en route to the Mediterranean and any evacuation from the Congo was likely to be handled by U.S. Special operations forces in aircraft from Europe, he told reporters.
